Functions of two variables are a vital component in the development of the calculus. Thus, multiple representations of functions are stressed: numerical, symbolic, verbal and graphical. The exponential function is introduced since it is so fundamental to many natural phenomena. Also, the idea of a limit of a function is thoroughly studied, emphasizing the classical tangent and velocity problems -- the study of the derivative. These two quantities are the two most compelling representations of the material covered in this course -- that of the differential calculus. Applications are very much a part of this course. Problems pertaining to the graphing of functions, related rates, and minimum and maximum are studied. The course concludes with a brief introduction to the second major branch of the calculus: the problem of finding antiderivatives. Course Philosophy: Building on the ideas and techniques of calculus in MATH 1A and MATH 1B, this course introduces students to the application of derivatives and integrals to studying infinite series. Of particular interest is the way in which calculating definite integrals, not possible using elementary techniques, can be approximated using infinite series. Students are then introduced to lines, planes and vectors in three dimensions as well as alternate coordinate systems for representing them. At this juncture, students learn to compare and contrast the strengths and weaknesses of the various coordinate systems, and to develop ideas regarding their appropriate usage. Finally, students are introduced to derivatives and integrals of vector functions, and apply these ideas to arc length, curvature, and motion in space. Students are also introduced to parametric equations of curves. Here, students experience for the first time that the ideas of differentiation and integration are not limited to two dimensions, but can be generalized and studied in multi-dimensional format. Students are then introduced to lines, planes and vectors in three dimensions as well as alternate coordinate systems for representing them. Course Code: STAT C1000
Title: Introduction to Statistics
Department: Discipline 1 [Mathematics]
Units: 5.0
Prerequisites: Placement as determined by the college’s multiple measures assessment process or completion of a course taught at or above the level of intermediate algebra.
Description: Part 1: This course is an introduction to statistical thinking and processes, including methods and concepts for discovery and decision-making using data. Topics include descriptive statistics; probability and sampling distributions; statistical inference; correlation and linear regression; analysis of variance, chi-squared, and t-tests; and application of technology for statistical analysis including the interpretation of the relevance of the statistical findings. Students apply methods and processes to applications using data from a broad range of disciplines. Part 2: This course is also an introduction to data analysis, making use of graphical and numerical techniques to study patterns and departures from patterns. The student studies randomness with an emphasis on understanding variation collects information in the face of uncertainty, checks distributional assumptions, tests hypotheses, uses probability as a tool for anticipating what the distribution of data may look like under a set of assumptions, and uses appropriate statistical models to draw conclusions from data. The course introduces the student to applications in engineering, business, economics, medicine, education, social sciences, psychology, the sciences, and those pertaining to issues of contemporary interest. The use of technology (computers or graphing calculators) will be required in certain applications. Where appropriate, the contributions to the development of statistics by men and women from diverse cultures will be introduced. This Statistics course is a required lower-division course for students majoring or minoring in many disciplines, such as data science, nursing, business, and others.

Certificates – Overview and Requirements
        
    
    
    
    
        
            
    
De Anza College offers several types of certificates, as described in this section. In general

 
	
Students must complete the required courses as prescribed to earn a certificate.

	
There is no limit on how many certificates a student can earn.

	
Students should check with a counselor and the department offering the desired certificate to get help with planning

Certificates of Achievement and Certificates of Achievement-Advanced

Certificates of Achievement and Certificates of Achievement-Advanced are designed for students interested in instructional
	programs with a high degree of specialization. These academic certificate programs vary in length and generally require
	less than two years of full-time study to complete. If the student prefers, they may be completed on a part-time basis.


Many of these programs have been designed on the ladder concept, so that courses taken to meet requirements for a Certificate
	of Achievement can also count toward some of the requirements for the higher-unit Certificate of Achievement-Advanced, and
	courses required for the Certificate of Achievement-Advanced courses can be applied toward some of the requirements for

De Anza was established in Cupertino on Sept. 11, 1967, as the Foothill Junior College District worked to meet local community demand for a second campus. Planning for the new college began soon after the district’s first campus, Foothill College, launched in temporary quarters in 1958 and filled to capacity after moving in 1961 to its permanent location in Los Altos Hills. Just four years after approving a $10.4 million bond measure for Foothill, community members readily voted in favor of a second bond measure, in the amount of $14 million, to build De Anza College.


De Anza was constructed on 112 acres of what was once a turn-of-the-century wine producing estate that the district purchased for $1.1 million. Guiding principles for the new college called for creating an “open door” institution to serve students with a wide variety of abilities, aptitudes and interests; an atmosphere of “friendly informality between faculty members and students”; and a campus that conveyed a sense of “quiet dignity” and “higher learning.”


Over the decades, De Anza’s enrollment has grown from 3,000 students in its first year to nearly 18,000 today.

History of De Anza College
        
    
    
    
    
        
             
        
    
    
    
        
            
    
De Anza was established in Cupertino on Sept. 11, 1967, as the Foothill Junior College District worked to meet local community demand for a second campus. Planning for the new college began soon after the district’s first campus, Foothill College, launched in temporary quarters in 1958 and filled to capacity after moving in 1961 to its permanent location in Los Altos Hills. Just four years after approving a $10.4 million bond measure for Foothill, community members readily voted in favor of a second bond measure, in the amount of $14 million, to build De Anza College.


De Anza was constructed on 112 acres of what was once a turn-of-the-century wine producing estate that the district purchased for $1.1 million. Guiding principles for the new college called for creating an “open door” institution to serve students with a wide variety of abilities, aptitudes and interests; an atmosphere of “friendly informality between faculty members and students”; and a campus that conveyed a sense of “quiet dignity” and “higher learning.”


Over the decades, De Anza’s enrollment has grown from 3,000 students in its first year to nearly 18,000 today.

California Residents

Students who have established California residency for at least one year and a day prior to the term in which they wish to enroll, and have met residency conditions required by state regulations, may enroll as California residents for tuition purposes.

Nonresidents

California residents – and residents of other states or territories – must pay nonresident tuition if they have not resided in California for one year and a day prior to the term in which they wish to enroll.

A unit is the standard measurement of college and university work. One unit equals one hour of classroom work in most classes, predominantly those in lecture or lecture-discussion formats.

De Anza was established in Cupertino on Sept. 11, 1967, as the Foothill Junior College District worked to meet local community demand for a second campus. Planning for the new college began soon after the district’s first campus, Foothill College, launched in temporary quarters in 1958 and filled to capacity after moving in 1961 to its permanent location in Los Altos Hills. Just four years after approving a $10.4 million bond measure for Foothill, community members readily voted in favor of a second bond measure, in the amount of $14 million, to build De Anza College.


De Anza was constructed on 112 acres of what was once a turn-of-the-century wine producing estate that the district purchased for $1.1 million. Guiding principles for the new college called for creating an “open door” institution to serve students with a wide variety of abilities, aptitudes and interests; an atmosphere of “friendly informality between faculty members and students”; and a campus that conveyed a sense of “quiet dignity” and “higher learning.”

De Anza was established in Cupertino on Sept. 11, 1967, as the Foothill Junior College District worked to meet local community demand for a second campus. Planning for the new college began soon after the district’s first campus, Foothill College, launched in temporary quarters in 1958 and filled to capacity after moving in 1961 to its permanent location in Los Altos Hills. Just four years after approving a $10.4 million bond measure for Foothill, community members readily voted in favor of a second bond measure, in the amount of $14 million, to build De Anza College.


De Anza was constructed on 112 acres of what was once a turn-of-the-century wine producing estate that the district purchased for $1.1 million. Guiding principles for the new college called for creating an “open door” institution to serve students with a wide variety of abilities, aptitudes and interests; an atmosphere of “friendly informality between faculty members and students”; and a campus that conveyed a sense of “quiet dignity” and “higher learning.”


Over the decades, De Anza’s enrollment has grown from 3,000 students in its first year to nearly 18,000 today.

        units of an audited course for students enrolled in 15 or more quarter units for credit.

No student auditing a course shall be permitted to change his or her enrollment to receive credit for the course.
        Course audits may not be approved to override repetition rules.

        After that, auditors may enroll on a space available basis.

        Instructors have no obligation to grade tests or other class assignments submitted by an auditor; however, an

Student Learning Outcomes: Analyze and synthesize the concepts of limits, continuity, and differentiation from a graphical, numerical, analytical and verbal approach, using correct notation and mathematical precision. Evaluate the behavior of graphs in the context of limits, continuity and differentiability. Course Philosophy: This is the first course in the calculus sequence. As such, it develops the foundations from which MATH 1B-1D are built. Functions of two variables are a vital component in the development of the calculus. Thus, multiple representations of functions are stressed: numerical, symbolic, verbal and graphical. The exponential function is introduced since it is so fundamental to many natural phenomena. Also, the idea of a limit of a function is thoroughly studied, emphasizing the classical tangent and velocity problems -- the study of the derivative. These two quantities are the two most compelling representations of the material covered in this course -- that of the differential calculus. Applications are very much a part of this course. Problems pertaining to the graphing of functions, related rates, and minimum and maximum are studied. The course concludes with a brief introduction to the second major branch of the calculus: the problem of finding antiderivatives. This sets the stage for the development of the integral calculus in MATH 1B. This outline contains historical notes relevant to the material covered in the sections they appear. Course Philosophy: This course introduces the problem of finding the area under the graph of a function over an interval-first by approximating the areas of rectangles fitted in the desired region, and then by invoking limits to find the exact area. The two seemingly unrelated problems - one, of finding the slope of the tangent line and two, of finding the area under a curve - are in fact very intimately related, as the student learns, through the fundamental theorem of calculus. In fact, differentiation (MATH 1A) and integration (MATH 1B) are inverse processes. The solution to the area problem is useful in solving other problems. Course Philosophy: Building on the ideas and techniques of calculus in MATH 1A and MATH 1B, this course introduces students to the application of derivatives and integrals to studying infinite series. Of particular interest is the way in which calculating definite integrals, not possible using elementary techniques, can be approximated using infinite series. Students are then introduced to lines, planes and vectors in three dimensions as well as alternate coordinate systems for representing them. At this juncture, students learn to compare and contrast the strengths and weaknesses of the various coordinate systems, and to develop ideas regarding their appropriate usage. Finally, students are introduced to derivatives and integrals of vector functions, and apply these ideas to arc length, curvature, and motion in space. Students are also introduced to parametric equations of curves. Here, students experience for the first time that the ideas of differentiation and integration are not limited to two dimensions, but can be generalized and studied in multi-dimensional format. Students are then introduced to lines, planes and vectors in three dimensions as well as alternate coordinate systems for representing them. Students are also introduced to parametric equations of curves. Here, students experience for the first time that the ideas of differentiation and integration are not limited to two dimensions, but can be generalized and studied in multi-dimensional format. Description: Part 1: This course is an introduction to statistical thinking and processes, including methods and concepts for discovery and decision-making using data. Topics include descriptive statistics; probability and sampling distributions; statistical inference; correlation and linear regression; analysis of variance, chi-squared, and t-tests; and application of technology for statistical analysis including the interpretation of the relevance of the statistical findings. Students apply methods and processes to applications using data from a broad range of disciplines. Part 2: This course is also an introduction to data analysis, making use of graphical and numerical techniques to study patterns and departures from patterns. The student studies randomness with an emphasis on understanding variation collects information in the face of uncertainty, checks distributional assumptions, tests hypotheses, uses probability as a tool for anticipating what the distribution of data may look like under a set of assumptions, and uses appropriate statistical models to draw conclusions from data. The course introduces the student to applications in engineering, business, economics, medicine, education, social sciences, psychology, the sciences, and those pertaining to issues of contemporary interest. The use of technology (computers or graphing calculators) will be required in certain applications. Where appropriate, the contributions to the development of statistics by men and women from diverse cultures will be introduced. This Statistics course is a required lower-division course for students majoring or minoring in many disciplines, such as data science, nursing, business, and others.

History of De Anza College
        
    
    
    
    
        
             
        
    
    
    
        
            
    
De Anza was established in Cupertino on Sept. 11, 1967, as the Foothill Junior College District worked to meet local community demand for a second campus. Planning for the new college began soon after the district’s first campus, Foothill College, launched in temporary quarters in 1958 and filled to capacity after moving in 1961 to its permanent location in Los Altos Hills. Just four years after approving a $10.4 million bond measure for Foothill, community members readily voted in favor of a second bond measure, in the amount of $14 million, to build De Anza College.


De Anza was constructed on 112 acres of what was once a turn-of-the-century wine producing estate that the district purchased for $1.1 million. Guiding principles for the new college called for creating an “open door” institution to serve students with a wide variety of abilities, aptitudes and interests; an atmosphere of “friendly informality between faculty members and students”; and a campus that conveyed a sense of “quiet dignity” and “higher learning.”


Over the decades, De Anza’s enrollment has grown from 3,000 students in its first year to nearly 18,000 today.

History of De Anza College
        
    
    
    
    
        
             
        
    
    
    
        
            
    
De Anza was established in Cupertino on Sept. 11, 1967, as the Foothill Junior College District worked to meet local community demand for a second campus. Planning for the new college began soon after the district’s first campus, Foothill College, launched in temporary quarters in 1958 and filled to capacity after moving in 1961 to its permanent location in Los Altos Hills. Just four years after approving a $10.4 million bond measure for Foothill, community members readily voted in favor of a second bond measure, in the amount of $14 million, to build De Anza College.


De Anza was constructed on 112 acres of what was once a turn-of-the-century wine producing estate that the district purchased for $1.1 million. Guiding principles for the new college called for creating an “open door” institution to serve students with a wide variety of abilities, aptitudes and interests; an atmosphere of “friendly informality between faculty members and students”; and a campus that conveyed a sense of “quiet dignity” and “higher learning.”


Over the decades, De Anza’s enrollment has grown from 3,000 students in its first year to nearly 18,000 today.

Extended Opportunity Programs and Services (EOPS) provides support services for economically and academically disadvantaged students. Services include academic and personal counseling; assistance in completing admission, registration and financial aid forms; early registration; university transfer services; and assistance with the cost of books, transportation and other educational expenses.

As part of EOPS, the Cooperative Agencies Resources for Education (CARE) program provides additional support services to single parents receiving Temporary Assistance for Needy Families. CARE students receive academic and personal counseling, early registration and financial assistance with child care, books and transportation.

EOPS also includes the NextUp program, which provides all EOPS services and additional resources designed specifically for students who are current and former foster youth. The Guardian Scholars program, housed in the EOPS office, also serves students who are current or foster youth.

Unit Load Limitations
        
    
    
    
    
        
            
    
A normal class load is 12-17 units. Students are classified as full-time if they are taking at least 12 units.

New students may not take more than 21.5 units during their first quarter at De Anza without the approval of the dean of Counseling and Disability Support Programs and Services.

Continuing students may enroll in more than 21.5 units (including physical education and labs) if they have met the following conditions:

 
	Completed a minimum of 18 units in the preceding quarter at De Anza

	Have not withdrawn from more than one class in the preceding quarter, and 

	Have a cumulative GPA of at least 3.0

 
Students meeting the above criteria who wish to enroll in more than 21.5 units must petition through their counselor, by meeting with their counselor to complete the Exceeding Units e-form. Units of Academic Credit
        
    
    
    
    
        
            
    
A unit is the standard measurement of college and university work. One unit equals one hour of classroom work in most classes, predominantly those in lecture or lecture-discussion formats. 

Students should expect to spend two hours of outside preparation for each one hour spent in class. Laboratory classes have three hours of work per week per unit. (Specialized performance classes such as athletics, drama and music require more than three hours per week per unit.)

Quarter units are equal to two-thirds of a semester unit. Conversely, a semester unit is equal to one and a half quarter units.

De Anza was established in Cupertino on Sept. 11, 1967, as the Foothill Junior College District worked to meet local community demand for a second campus. Planning for the new college began soon after the district’s first campus, Foothill College, launched in temporary quarters in 1958 and filled to capacity after moving in 1961 to its permanent location in Los Altos Hills. Just four years after approving a $10.4 million bond measure for Foothill, community members readily voted in favor of a second bond measure, in the amount of $14 million, to build De Anza College.


De Anza was constructed on 112 acres of what was once a turn-of-the-century wine producing estate that the district purchased for $1.1 million. Guiding principles for the new college called for creating an “open door” institution to serve students with a wide variety of abilities, aptitudes and interests; an atmosphere of “friendly informality between faculty members and students”; and a campus that conveyed a sense of “quiet dignity” and “higher learning.”


Over the decades, De Anza’s enrollment has grown from 3,000 students in its first year to nearly 18,000 today.

De Anza was established in Cupertino on Sept. 11, 1967, as the Foothill Junior College District worked to meet local community demand for a second campus. Planning for the new college began soon after the district’s first campus, Foothill College, launched in temporary quarters in 1958 and filled to capacity after moving in 1961 to its permanent location in Los Altos Hills. Just four years after approving a $10.4 million bond measure for Foothill, community members readily voted in favor of a second bond measure, in the amount of $14 million, to build De Anza College.


De Anza was constructed on 112 acres of what was once a turn-of-the-century wine producing estate that the district purchased for $1.1 million. Guiding principles for the new college called for creating an “open door” institution to serve students with a wide variety of abilities, aptitudes and interests; an atmosphere of “friendly informality between faculty members and students”; and a campus that conveyed a sense of “quiet dignity” and “higher learning.”


Over the decades, De Anza’s enrollment has grown from 3,000 students in its first year to nearly 18,000 today.

Auditing Classes
        
    
    
    
    
        
            
    
Students who have satisfactorily completed a class for the maximum allowable times may be able to audit a class for
        no credit.

A nonrefundable fee of $10 per unit is assessed for audited classes; however, there is no charge for the first five
        units of an audited course for students enrolled in 15 or more quarter units for credit.

No student auditing a course shall be permitted to change his or her enrollment to receive credit for the course.
        Course audits may not be approved to override repetition rules.

During the first two weeks of class, students enrolling for credit will have registration priority over auditors.
        After that, auditors may enroll on a space available basis.

Auditing carries no privilege other than to attend classes. Students do not receive credit for an audited course.
        Instructors have no obligation to grade tests or other class assignments submitted by an auditor; however, an
        instructor may permit an auditor to participate in class discussions.

Students wishing to audit should contact the instructor. If the instructor approves, they will submit the necessary

Course Philosophy: This is the first course in the calculus sequence. As such, it develops the foundations from which MATH 1B-1D are built. Functions of two variables are a vital component in the development of the calculus. Thus, multiple representations of functions are stressed: numerical, symbolic, verbal and graphical. The exponential function is introduced since it is so fundamental to many natural phenomena. Also, the idea of a limit of a function is thoroughly studied, emphasizing the classical tangent and velocity problems -- the study of the derivative. Problems pertaining to the graphing of functions, related rates, and minimum and maximum are studied. The course concludes with a brief introduction to the second major branch of the calculus: the problem of finding antiderivatives.    - CIS 22A is designed primarily for computer science and related transfer majors.
   - CIS 22B is targeted towards software engineering and computer science students.

In summary, CIS 22A is an introductory C++ programming course, while CIS 22B is an intermediate-level course that builds upon the concepts covered in CIS 22A.

Registered Nursing Program

The Associate Degree Nursing Program is approved by the California Board of Registered Nursing. The RN graduate is eligible to take the California State Board Examination for licensing (NCLEX - RN). Students are admitted to this program during the fall, winter and spring quarters. The majority of courses are scheduled in the daytime. Generally, the program is not scheduled in the summer session. Upon admission, the program takes six quarters to complete, not counting prerequisites.


LVN Transition to RN Nursing Program

The LVN Transition to RN graduate is eligible to take the California State Board Examination for licensing (NCLEX - RN). Students are admitted throughout the year as advanced placements. The majority of courses are scheduled in the daytime. Generally, the program is not scheduled in the summer session. Upon admission, the program takes at least three quarters to complete, not counting prerequisites. A current California LVN license and IV certification are required.


Advanced Placement for Students with Prior Nursing Education

Students are admitted to advanced placement during the fall, winter or spring quarter on a space-available basis only. Placement depends on prior nursing education.

De Anza was established in Cupertino on Sept. 11, 1967, as the Foothill Junior College District worked to meet local community demand for a second campus. Planning for the new college began soon after the district’s first campus, Foothill College, launched in temporary quarters in 1958 and filled to capacity after moving in 1961 to its permanent location in Los Altos Hills. Just four years after approving a $10.4 million bond measure for Foothill, community members readily voted in favor of a second bond measure, in the amount of $14 million, to build De Anza College.


De Anza was constructed on 112 acres of what was once a turn-of-the-century wine producing estate that the district purchased for $1.1 million. Guiding principles for the new college called for creating an “open door” institution to serve students with a wide variety of abilities, aptitudes and interests; an atmosphere of “friendly informality between faculty members and students”; and a campus that conveyed a sense of “quiet dignity” and “higher learning.”


Over the decades, De Anza’s enrollment has grown from 3,000 students in its first year to nearly 18,000 today.

Students should regularly perform a degree audit through Degree Works to monitor their own progress in reaching educational goals and meeting graduation requirements. It's also recommended that students consult with a counselor or academic adviser.

History of De Anza College
        
    
    
    
    
        
             
        
    
    
    
        
            
    
De Anza was established in Cupertino on Sept. 11, 1967, as the Foothill Junior College District worked to meet local community demand for a second campus. Planning for the new college began soon after the district’s first campus, Foothill College, launched in temporary quarters in 1958 and filled to capacity after moving in 1961 to its permanent location in Los Altos Hills. Just four years after approving a $10.4 million bond measure for Foothill, community members readily voted in favor of a second bond measure, in the amount of $14 million, to build De Anza College.


De Anza was constructed on 112 acres of what was once a turn-of-the-century wine producing estate that the district purchased for $1.1 million. Guiding principles for the new college called for creating an “open door” institution to serve students with a wide variety of abilities, aptitudes and interests; an atmosphere of “friendly informality between faculty members and students”; and a campus that conveyed a sense of “quiet dignity” and “higher learning.”


Over the decades, De Anza’s enrollment has grown from 3,000 students in its first year to nearly 18,000 today.

1. The De Anza College Promise provides eligible first-time college students with:
   - At least one year (three quarters) of free tuition, and possibly two years depending on state funding
   - Free transportation with the VTA SmartPass

2. To qualify, students must:
   - Be a first-time college student
   - Enroll full-time (at least 12 units per quarter)
   - Maintain at least a 2.0 GPA

3. The program is open to California residents or those exempted from nonresident tuition, including students with AB 540 status.

4. Students may also qualify for additional tuition coverage through other financial aid programs like the California College Promise Grant fee waiver.

Based on the information provided in the documents, the key residency requirements for in-state (California resident) tuition at De Anza College are:

1. Physical Presence:
   - The student must be physically present in California for at least one year and one day prior to the residence determination date (first day of the term) to be classified as a California resident.
   - Physical presence in California solely for educational purposes does not establish residency, regardless of the length of presence.

2. Intent:
   - The student must demonstrate the intent to make California their permanent home and residence.
   - Intent can be shown through supporting evidence such as a California driver's license, voter registration, professional licenses, property ownership, bank statements, and continuous presence in California.

3. Financial Independence:
   - If the student is classified as a non-resident, they may be able to establish residency if they have been financially independent and met the requirements of California Code of Regulations 54020 for one year prior to the residence determination date.

4. Exceptions:
   - Certain individuals, such as active duty military members and their dependents, as well as newly arrived immigrants, refugees, and asylum seekers, may be eligible for in-state tuition rates even if they have not been in California for one year and one day.

The documents indicate that the student has the burden of proof to clearly demonstrate both physical presence in California and the intent to establish California residency in order to qualify for in-state tuition rates.

Units of Academic Credit
        
    
    
    
    
        
            
    
A unit is the standard measurement of college and university work. One unit equals one hour of classroom work in most classes, predominantly those in lecture or lecture-discussion formats. 

Students should expect to spend two hours of outside preparation for each one hour spent in class. Laboratory classes have three hours of work per week per unit. (Specialized performance classes such as athletics, drama and music require more than three hours per week per unit.)

Quarter units are equal to two-thirds of a semester unit. Conversely, a semester unit is equal to one and a half quarter units.

Based on the information provided in the documents, here are the key points regarding refunds at De Anza College:

1. Refunds for dropped classes:
- You can only get a refund if you drop a class before the drop deadline, which varies for each class. You can find the drop deadline for your specific classes on MyPortal.
- If you drop a class after the drop deadline, you generally cannot get a refund, unless the college canceled or rescheduled the class, or you failed to meet a prerequisite.
- The college may withhold a $10 service charge when processing the refund, except for classes dropped before the start of the term.

2. Refunds for out-of-state and foreign students:
- Out-of-state and foreign tuition will only be refunded for classes dropped before the drop deadline.

3. Refunds for parking fees:
- Parking fees will not be refunded after the second week of the quarter (first week of summer session), unless the college cancels all classes. You must return your parking decal to the campus police substation.

4. Requesting a refund:
- To request a refund, you need to drop the class through MyPortal and then submit a refund request through MyPortal.

Based on the information provided in the documents, here are the key steps to apply for the De Anza College Promise:

1. Submit the FAFSA (Free Application for Federal Student Aid) or the California Dream Act Application (CADAA) by August 31. Be sure to list De Anza College on the application.

6. Meet with a counselor if you need any assistance or have additional questions about the application process or eligibility requirements.

The key is to complete the FAFSA/CADAA, apply for admission, and enroll full-time by the deadlines to take advantage of the De Anza College Promise benefits, which include at least one year of free tuition and free transportation with the VTA SmartPass. History of De Anza College
        
    
    
    
    
        
             
        
    
    
    
        
            
    
De Anza was established in Cupertino on Sept. 11, 1967, as the Foothill Junior College District worked to meet local community demand for a second campus. Planning for the new college began soon after the district’s first campus, Foothill College, launched in temporary quarters in 1958 and filled to capacity after moving in 1961 to its permanent location in Los Altos Hills. Just four years after approving a $10.4 million bond measure for Foothill, community members readily voted in favor of a second bond measure, in the amount of $14 million, to build De Anza College.


De Anza was constructed on 112 acres of what was once a turn-of-the-century wine producing estate that the district purchased for $1.1 million. De Anza was established in Cupertino on Sept. 11, 1967, as the Foothill Junior College District worked to meet local community demand for a second campus. Planning for the new college began soon after the district’s first campus, Foothill College, launched in temporary quarters in 1958 and filled to capacity after moving in 1961 to its permanent location in Los Altos Hills. Just four years after approving a $10.4 million bond measure for Foothill, community members readily voted in favor of a second bond measure, in the amount of $14 million, to build De Anza College.


De Anza was constructed on 112 acres of what was once a turn-of-the-century wine producing estate that the district purchased for $1.1 million. Guiding principles for the new college called for creating an “open door” institution to serve students with a wide variety of abilities, aptitudes and interests; an atmosphere of “friendly informality between faculty members and students”; and a campus that conveyed a sense of “quiet dignity” and “higher learning.”


Over the decades, De Anza’s enrollment has grown from 3,000 students in its first year to nearly 18,000 today.

Based on the information provided in the documents, here are the key points regarding retaking a class you have already passed to improve your GPA:

1. You generally cannot repeat a course if you received a grade of C or better, unless you can show documented proof of extenuating circumstances such as a significant lapse of time (at least 3 years), a legal requirement for employment/licensing, a disability requiring accommodation, or other extenuating circumstances.

2. Courses designated as "repeatable" in the course descriptions can be repeated, but there is usually a limit of 6 enrollments total, including any times you received a substandard grade or W.

3. If you received a substandard grade (D+, D, D-, F, NC or NP) in a course, you may be able to petition to have that substandard grade excluded from your GPA calculation after you successfully complete an equivalent course at another accredited college/university. This is called "substandard work alleviation."

4. However, alleviating a substandard grade with a subsequent Pass/No Pass grade is not permitted, as it does not improve your GPA. The substandard grade will still remain on your transcript.

So in summary, you generally cannot just retake a course you've already passed with a C or better to improve your GPA, unless there are documented extenuating circumstances. The options would be to either repeat a "repeatable" course, or pursue substandard work alleviation if you received a substandard grade initially.

I'd recommend consulting with a counselor to discuss your specific situation and options. The Admissions and Records office can also provide more details on the policies and procedures.

Based on the information provided in the documents, here is what happens if you skip a quarter at De Anza College:

1. Continuous Enrollment (Document 1):
   - For determining your catalog rights and degree/certificate eligibility requirements, you need to maintain continuous enrollment.
   - Continuous enrollment means taking at least 2 quarters per academic year at De Anza or Foothill College.
   - A single "W" (Withdrawal) grade in a term qualifies as enrollment for that term.
   - Skipping a quarter would break your continuous enrollment.

2. Refund Policy (Document 2):
   - If you drop a class after the first 2 weeks (or 10% of a shorter course), you generally cannot get a refund, unless the college canceled or rescheduled the class.

3. Academic and Progress Notice (Documents 3 and 5):
   - Skipping a quarter would not directly impact your academic or progress notice status, as those are evaluated based on your cumulative GPA and completion rates.
   - However, breaking continuous enrollment could potentially impact your eligibility for financial aid, veterans benefits, or participation in campus programs, as mentioned in Document 5.

In summary, skipping a quarter at De Anza College would break your continuous enrollment, which could affect your catalog rights, degree/certificate eligibility, and potentially your eligibility for certain financial aid and campus programs. It's best to maintain continuous enrollment if possible. If you have any other specific questions, you can check the college website at deanza.edu or speak with an academic counselor.

These two quantities are the two most compelling representations of the material covered in this course -- that of the differential calculus. Applications are very much a part of this course. Problems pertaining to the graphing of functions, related rates, and minimum and maximum are studied. The course concludes with a brief introduction to the second major branch of the calculus: the problem of finding antiderivatives. This sets the stage for the development of the integral calculus in MATH 1B. This outline contains historical notes relevant to the material covered in the sections they appear. CIS 22A is "Beginning Programming Methodologies in C++" and CIS 22B is "Intermediate Programming Methodologies in C++".

CIS 22A covers fundamental programming constructs and introduces object-oriented programming, with an emphasis on structured procedural programming. It aims to teach problem-solving using C++.

CIS 22B focuses on a systematic approach to designing, constructing, and managing computer programs, emphasizing design, programming style, documentation, testing, and debugging. *   Completed a minimum of 18 units in the preceding quarter at De Anza
*   Have not withdrawn from more than one class in the preceding quarter
*   Have a cumulative GPA of at least 3.0

Students meeting these criteria who wish to enroll in more than 21.5 units must petition through their counselor by completing the Exceeding Units e-form. Petitions to enroll in more than 27 units will be referred to the Appeal Review Committee for a final determination.

During summer sessions, students may enroll in a maximum of 15 units, including physical education classes and labs. To exceed the 15-unit limit, students must meet with a counselor to complete a special petition form. Petitions to enroll in more than 18 units during summer sessions will be referred to the Appeal Review Committee for a final determination.

For more information, please visit deanza.edu.

De Anza was established in Cupertino on Sept. 11, 1967, as the Foothill Junior College District worked to meet local community demand for a second campus. Planning for the new college began soon after the district’s first campus, Foothill College, launched in temporary quarters in 1958 and filled to capacity after moving in 1961 to its permanent location in Los Altos Hills. Just four years after approving a $10.4 million bond measure for Foothill, community members readily voted in favor of a second bond measure, in the amount of $14 million, to build De Anza College.


De Anza was constructed on 112 acres of what was once a turn-of-the-century wine producing estate that the district purchased for $1.1 million. Guiding principles for the new college called for creating an “open door” institution to serve students with a wide variety of abilities, aptitudes and interests; an atmosphere of “friendly informality between faculty members and students”; and a campus that conveyed a sense of “quiet dignity” and “higher learning.”


Over the decades, De Anza’s enrollment has grown from 3,000 students in its first year to nearly 18,000 today.

History of De Anza College
        
    
    
    
    
        
             
        
    
    
    
        
            
    
De Anza was established in Cupertino on Sept. 11, 1967, as the Foothill Junior College District worked to meet local community demand for a second campus. Planning for the new college began soon after the district’s first campus, Foothill College, launched in temporary quarters in 1958 and filled to capacity after moving in 1961 to its permanent location in Los Altos Hills. Just four years after approving a $10.4 million bond measure for Foothill, community members readily voted in favor of a second bond measure, in the amount of $14 million, to build De Anza College.


De Anza was constructed on 112 acres of what was once a turn-of-the-century wine producing estate that the district purchased for $1.1 million. Guiding principles for the new college called for creating an “open door” institution to serve students with a wide variety of abilities, aptitudes and interests; an atmosphere of “friendly informality between faculty members and students”; and a campus that conveyed a sense of “quiet dignity” and “higher learning.”


Over the decades, De Anza’s enrollment has grown from 3,000 students in its first year to nearly 18,000 today.

google/gemini-2.5-flash.answer:
De Anza College assigns registration dates based on priority groups, following state and local regulations. These groups are designed to help new students start well and reward continuing students making progress toward their goals.

To qualify for priority registration, students generally need to:
*   Declare a major (not "Undecided").
*   Select a goal of transfer, degree, or certificate.
*   Complete the assessment process.
*   Complete orientation.
*   Create an educational plan (abbreviated for new students, comprehensive for continuing students).

Additionally, to receive priority registration, students cannot have completed more than 150 quarter units in degree-applicable courses (W and I grades, pre-collegiate English, ESL, and Math classes do not count toward this limit).

Here's a general overview of how some priority groups are ordered:

*   **Group 1:** Veterans, foster youth, DSPS, EOPS, CalWorks, student parents (who meet specific criteria), and Rising Scholars students who have completed orientation, assessment, and an educational plan.
*   **Group 2:** Student athletes who have selected an educational goal of transfer, degree or certificate, declared a major, have not been on probation for two consecutive terms, and completed orientation, assessment, and an educational plan.
*   **Continuing Students:** Those who have selected an educational goal of transfer, degree or certificate, and declared a major and have not been on probation for two consecutive terms.

Specific registration dates for these groups vary by quarter. For example, for a recent quarter:
*   Group 1 registration opened on April 27.
*   Group 2 registration opened on April 28.
*   Group 3 registration opened on April 29.

You can register from your assigned start date through the end of the add/drop period. After completing all the necessary steps, allow time for your record to be updated to reflect your priority registration status.

For more detailed information, including specific dates for upcoming quarters and how to register, please visit deanza.edu.

Students who have established California residency for at least one year and a day prior to the term in which they wish to enroll, and have met residency conditions required by state regulations, may enroll as California residents for tuition purposes.

Nonresidents

De Anza's six Villages are communities for students, faculty, and staff that are organized around related academic interests and majors. They are part of the Guided Pathways initiative, which aims to provide clear paths for students to achieve their academic goals.

Here's how they work:
*   **Community and Support:** Villages offer a way to connect with the De Anza community, providing a supportive network with shared academic interests. Each Village has a designated Success Team of academic counselors and staff members.
*   **Resources and Services:** Villages offer resources, services, and activities relevant to students' majors and career goals. This includes peer mentoring, career guidance, and program maps that outline quarter-by-quarter plans for degrees, certificates, or transfer.
*   **Village Centers:** Students can connect with their Village community by visiting designated Village Centers on campus. These physical spaces are where students can study, speak with a counselor, or socialize with friends. They are marked by brightly colored signs and are included on campus maps.
*   **Online Access:** Students can also connect with their Village online by visiting their Village webpage or logging into their Village site on Canvas, the college's online learning platform.
*   **Events:** Villages host a variety of events throughout the year, such as career panels, transfer panels, guest speakers, workshops, games, and movie days. Weekly "hangouts" are also offered for conversation. These events are open to all students, regardless of their Village affiliation.
*   **Counseling:** Students are encouraged to work with counselors who are part of their Village.

The six Villages are:
*   Artistic Expression Village
*   Business and Finance Village
*   Health and Life Sciences Village
*   Language and Communication Village
*   Physical Sciences and Technology Village
*   Social Sciences and Humanities Village

All students are encouraged to join a Village. For more information, you can visit deanza.edu/villages.

History of De Anza College
        
    
    
    
    
        
             
        
    
    
    
        
            
    
De Anza was established in Cupertino on Sept. 11, 1967, as the Foothill Junior College District worked to meet local community demand for a second campus. Planning for the new college began soon after the district’s first campus, Foothill College, launched in temporary quarters in 1958 and filled to capacity after moving in 1961 to its permanent location in Los Altos Hills. Just four years after approving a $10.4 million bond measure for Foothill, community members readily voted in favor of a second bond measure, in the amount of $14 million, to build De Anza College.


De Anza was constructed on 112 acres of what was once a turn-of-the-century wine producing estate that the district purchased for $1.1 million. Guiding principles for the new college called for creating an “open door” institution to serve students with a wide variety of abilities, aptitudes and interests; an atmosphere of “friendly informality between faculty members and students”; and a campus that conveyed a sense of “quiet dignity” and “higher learning.”


Over the decades, De Anza’s enrollment has grown from 3,000 students in its first year to nearly 18,000 today.

History of De Anza College
        
    
    
    
    
        
             
        
    
    
    
        
            
    
De Anza was established in Cupertino on Sept. 11, 1967, as the Foothill Junior College District worked to meet local community demand for a second campus. Planning for the new college began soon after the district’s first campus, Foothill College, launched in temporary quarters in 1958 and filled to capacity after moving in 1961 to its permanent location in Los Altos Hills. Just four years after approving a $10.4 million bond measure for Foothill, community members readily voted in favor of a second bond measure, in the amount of $14 million, to build De Anza College.


De Anza was constructed on 112 acres of what was once a turn-of-the-century wine producing estate that the district purchased for $1.1 million. Guiding principles for the new college called for creating an “open door” institution to serve students with a wide variety of abilities, aptitudes and interests; an atmosphere of “friendly informality between faculty members and students”; and a campus that conveyed a sense of “quiet dignity” and “higher learning.”


Over the decades, De Anza’s enrollment has grown from 3,000 students in its first year to nearly 18,000 today.
